Unlike traditional models that rely on static utility functions, the lower level employs Neuro-Symbolic Agents to inject heuristic-driven bounded rationality, acting as a sandbox that exposes latent market vulnerabilities ignored by convex optimization. The upper level utilizes derivative-free Bayesian Optimization (BO) to autonomously navigate this non-differentiable cognitive feedback and discover a deterrence-based regulatory policy. Empirical evaluations using the real-world physical net-load dataset from Madeira Island substantiate the framework’s efficacy. The experiments validate that the optimized dynamic volatility tax operates effectively via deterrence, steering heuristic agents to voluntarily correct cognitive failures (e.g., converting speculative trading into a strategic retreat). This mechanism achieves a robust market equilibrium, reducing price volatility ( $\sigma _{\lambda }$ ) by 84.6% and successfully withstanding the unstructured behavioral unpredictability inherent in decentralized energy communities.

title: Enhancing Resilience of Power Distribution Systems Under Cyber-Physical Hybrid Attacks: A Coordinated Localization and Restoration Strategy With Feeder Automation
abstract: The widespread deployment of distributed feeder automation (DFA) has increased the vulnerability of power distribution systems to cyber-physical hybrid attacks. To enhance the resilience of power distribution systems under hybrid attacks, this paper proposes a two-stage integrated cyber-physical system (TICPS) recovery strategy. This strategy integrates hybrid attack localization and isolation, and cyber-physical collaborative restoration, while effectively coordinating multiple resources. In the first stage, a hybrid attack localization module is developed, incorporating an attack descriptive model and a network equivalent transformation method to accurately locate cyber and physical attacks. The localization results are then used to guide DFA to isolate attacked agents and line faults resulting from the attacks. In the second stage, a grid reconfiguration and island formation module is first proposed to achieve efficient load restoration while considering the operational constraints of DFA under a compromised cyber layer. Subsequently, a repair crew dispatch module is designed to optimize crew routing based on value functions of cyber-physical faulty components, thereby facilitating complete cyber-physical system recovery. To leverage sequentially restored and controllable resources during the repair process, a repair event-triggered mechanism is introduced to coordinate grid reconfiguration and crew dispatch. The effectiveness and scalability of the proposed strategy are validated through simulations on the IEEE 33-bus and IEEE 123-bus systems, which demonstrate promising results.

title: Distributed Resilient Power Control Strategy Against Data Injection Attacks in Wind Farms
abstract: With the increasing proportion of installed wind power capacity in the power grid, higher requirements are put forward for the cyber security technology of wind energy enterprises. However, due to problems such as incomplete construction and unstrict requirements, there exist many blind spots of cyber security in the current power monitoring system of wind energy enterprises. Data injection attacks targeting the communication pathway between the supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) system and the wind turbines will degrade the power generation of wind farms and lead to an imbalance in the power supply to the grid. To this end, this paper attempts to propose an observation and compensation based distributed resilient power control strategy to resist data injection attacks in the wind farm. The data injection threat model is formulated to characterize the behavior of tampering with the power information of wind turbines reported to the local controller and SCADA system, and an adaptive observer is proposed to observe the injected value in real-time, guiding the wind farm to balance the power generation. A distributed resilient power control strategy is developed to ensure the dynamic balance of expected power generation and the secure operation of wind farms. Extensive studies on a wind farm consisting of 9 wind turbines verify that the proposed method can eliminate the impact of data injection attacks and ensure the expected control performance of the wind farm.

title: Beyond Energy Trading: AI-Enhanced Peer-to-Peer Energy Bartering
abstract: Peer-to-peer energy trading supports efficient utilization of renewable energy but fails to address energy poverty and financial transaction barriers, particularly during economic or infrastructural crises. Consumers may lack funds or means to purchase energy or face difficulties in making transactions for various reasons, while producers may struggle to sell surplus energy through conventional markets. To overcome these challenges, energy bartering offers a promising non-monetary alternative by facilitating direct energy exchange among peers within smart grid environments. This paper proposes AI-P2P-EB, a novel artificial intelligence-enhanced peer-to-peer energy bartering algorithm that improves producer profitability and drives broader participation in decentralized energy systems. Three bartering algorithms and their influencing factors across two scenarios were analyzed. Using two real-world datasets, it is demonstrated that the studied bartering algorithms reduced reliance on the utility grid, saving up to 1,310 megawatt-hours, and bartered between 3.8 megawatt-hours to 1.9 gigawatt-hours. Energy bartering maximizes monetary benefits for peers when the grid does not buy all surplus energy. In contrast, when the grid buys surplus, consumer benefits outweigh producer gains, except in the centralized approach. Our findings categorize energy transactions based on driving incentives and demonstrate the superior performance of the AI-enhanced algorithm in increasing producer profits while maintaining a high amount of bartered energy.

title: Infrequent Control of Thermostatically Controlled Loads for Fast Power System Services
abstract: Controlling electric load aggregations enables the demand side to provide services to the grid. However, the feedback and actuation update rates of these loads could be limited by technical constraints. In this paper, we consider a frequency regulation application with thermostatically controlled loads, in which the underlying devices can only send feedback and be actuated at a rate that is slower than the reference signal being tracked. We develop a control approach to maximize the potential for providing fast power system services with limited feedback and actuation frequency. This approach balances computational effort and tracking accuracy by utilizing an aggregate representation of the controlled devices in a quadratic programming optimization problem. The trade-off between computational effort and tracking accuracy is explored by using a second much more complex controller that considers the dynamics of individual devices. The impact of imperfect reference signal forecasts is also analyzed.

title: Learning a Unified Feasibility--Cost Interface for Heterogeneous Flexible Resources
abstract: With the rapid proliferation of heterogeneous flexible resources (HFRs), such as microgrids and virtual power plants, hierarchical dispatch has become essential, making aggregate modeling a crucial foundation for resource coordination. Existing methods typically decouple the aggregate feasible region (AFR) of HFRs from the aggregate cost function (ACF). This separation isolates physical constraints from economic signals, preventing operators from quantifying the marginal value of flexibility and causing modeling redundancy. To solve this, we propose a feasibility-embedded aggregate cost function, unifying feasibility and cost into a strictly convex scalar interface. First, by implicitly representing physical limits as steep economic penalties, we recast the decoupled aggregation of AFR and ACF into a unified fitting problem. Second, a tailored multi-scale input-convex neural network is developed to resolve the inherent conflict between approximating smooth operational costs and capturing sharp feasibility barriers. Numerical results validate that the proposed interface achieves superior accuracy while maintaining a highly compact formulation.

title: Fuzzy Deep Reinforcement Learning-Based Space–Air–Ground Integration for Electric Power Emergency Communication
abstract: With the advancement of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and artificial intelligence, space-air-ground integration reshapes electric power emergency communication through coordinated resource scheduling. However, existing learning-based resource scheduling has slow convergence, local optimality, and poor quantifiable interpretability. In this paper, we propose a fuzzy deep reinforcement learning-based resource scheduling design, aiming to maximize the weighted sum of inspection and coverage utility minus backhaul delay cost by optimizing UAV path planning, backhaul routing, and flow control. It develops a multi-agent interactive deep fuzzy neuro actor critic mechanism for collaborative 3D path planning and a backpressure-aware approach for multi-hop data backhaul. Simulations in flooding areas show its superiority in real-time situational awareness, on-demand coverage, and fast inspection.

title: Microgrid Under-Frequency Load Shedding Strategy Integrating LMC-Shapley Value and Knowledge Distillation
abstract: As the final safeguard for maintaining microgrid stability, under-frequency load shedding (UFLS) can effectively prevent rapid frequency drops caused by system faults. However, a key challenge remains in how to fairly and effectively allocate load shedding across nodes to enhance overall system resilience. To address this issue, this paper proposes a microgrid UFLS strategy that integrates Shapley value with load multiplicity characteristics (LMC-Shapley) and knowledge distillation. The strategy first constructs a node contribution factor based on the load importance, economic loss from load shedding and frequency regulation effect. Then, based on the LMC-Shapley value method, the marginal contributions and allocation coefficients of each indicator are calculated to determine the load shedding amount for each node. To mitigate the computational complexity introduced by the LMC-Shapley method, a model lightweighting method based on knowledge distillation is proposed, allowing transfer of complex knowledge from a teacher model to a student model. Finally, based on the improved IEEE-37 node system microgrid model, the performance of the proposed strategy is verified. Simulation results reveal that the proposed strategy exhibits good frequency recovery performance.

title: Optimal Integrated Satellite-Terrestrial Network Design for Microgrid Clusters Under Wildfires
abstract: Wildfires pose a critical threat to microgrid clusters especially in mountainous and remote areas, degrading communication infrastructures and destroying system stability. To address this issue, this paper proposes a wildfire-oriented communication network design for resilient operation of microgrid clusters based on an integrated satellite-terrestrial network (ISTN). First, a disaster-aware reliability assessment model is developed to describe communication link availability by explicitly coupling wildfire evolution with link failure mechanisms. Second, based on the wildfire-induced link availability obtained from the reliability assessment model, a topology restoration model is formulated to maximize algebraic connectivity under limited satellite terminal deployment constraints, and an alternating optimization strategy based on the Fiedler vector (ALT-Fiedler) is proposed to solve the resulting mixed-integer spectral optimization problem. Third, based on the restored topology, a communication weight optimization model is established to characterize the trade-off between convergence performance and delay robustness, which is reformulated as a semidefinite programming problem (SDP) for solution. Finally, simulation results validate that the proposed method effectively restores communication connectivity under wildfire conditions with limited satellite terminals and enables reliable coordinated operation of microgrid clusters.

title: Reconnection-Time-Optimal Fractional-Chaotic SIR-Gossip Control for Resilient Microgrid Islanding and Reconnection
abstract: The rapid growth of distributed renewable generation and inverter-based resources has heightened the need for control strategies that guarantee both safety and freshness during microgrid islanding and reconnection, such as those used in real-time dynamic network environments. In the specific scenario of microgrid reconnection, existing schemes like randomized gossip, asynchronous gossip, and fractional-order consensus can not effectively exploit fractional memory and trust-SIR dynamics, leading to slow convergence and high reconnection time. In this paper, we propose a unified fractional-chaotic susceptible-infected-recovered (SIR)-Gossip controller (UFSC) to solve the existing problem of minimizing reconnection time while ensuring safety, integrity, and freshness. By optimizing the closed-form exponents and utilizing a co-designed framework of trust recovery, risk expansion, and consensus acceleration, our approach achieves provably minimal reconnection time and superior consensus accuracy. The experiment results demonstrate the advantages of our approach in improving reconnection time by up to 46% and reducing consensus error by up to 30%, outperforming traditional methods in terms of synchronization, trust recovery, and overall system performance.

title: Fréchet Power-Scenario Distance: A Measure for Evaluating Synthetic Data Across Multiple Time-Scales in Smart Grids
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence models for smart grids have advanced rapidly in recent years, and the synthetic data they produce can help mitigate limited data access caused by strict confidentiality constraints in power systems. A central challenge, however, is how to rigorously evaluate the quality of both the generative models and the synthetic time series they produce. Generic evaluation metrics are often not tailored to grid-specific requirements—such as multi-timescale temporal structure, cross-resolution consistency, and physically meaningful operating regimes—and therefore can yield misleading assessments. In this work, we propose a novel measure based on the Fréchet Distance (FD) estimated between two datasets in a power-centric learned feature space. Our approach embeds smart-grid time series using a hierarchical multi-resolution encoder trained on real grid data that encourages sensitivity to multi-timescale dynamics and resolution-consistent operational signatures. Across multiple use cases, the resulting Fr’echet Power-Scenario Distance (FPD) exposes temporal and physical mismatches more reliably and correlates with downstream task performance more strongly than conventional baselines, enabling more robust benchmarking of generative models for smart-grid data.

title: Robust State Estimation for Distribution Systems Based on Reinforcement-Learning-Assisted Memory-Augmented Deep Kalman Filter
abstract: Real-time monitoring and control of distribution networks rely on robust state estimation. The key challenges lie in maintaining the accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency of state estimation in the presence of bad measurement data and sudden changes in system states, particularly under limited sensor coverage. To overcome these challenges, this paper proposes a robust forecasting-aided state estimation method for distribution systems. The key methodology is a reinforcement-learning-assisted, memory-augmented, and gradient-fused deep Kalman filter. The proposed deep filter captures temporal patterns in state trajectories across multiple time steps, and fuses the prediction model’s gradient information into the state filtering stage for accurate uncertainty quantification. Based on normalized innovations, the proposed reinforcement learning-assisted method can also adjust the state filtering process to mitigate the impacts of bad data and state jumps on the estimation results with high efficiency. Extensive simulations are conducted on standard IEEE 34-node and 123-node test feeders with real-world load profiles and renewable generation data to demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method in terms of estimation accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency compared with a variety of state-of-the-art state estimation algorithms.

title: Distributed Fixed-Time Secondary Control for Microgrids With Communication Delays and Disturbances
abstract: The paper addresses the distributed secondary control (DSC) problem of the islanded microgrid composed of six distributed generators (DGs) with communication delay and external disturbances. Firstly, by utilizing the Artstein model reduction method, a distributed delay-compensated strategy is proposed to restore the voltage and frequency of each DG to reference values in a fixed time. Secondly, a novel sliding mode reaching law is designed to resist disturbances and accelerate convergence, thereby ensuring the sliding surface is reached within a fixed-time. Thirdly, the proposed approach integrates an event-triggered (ET) mechanism with an integral sliding mode surface, effectively conserving communication resources while avoiding Zeno behavior. In summary, the proposed delay-compensation strategy integrated with sliding mode control (SMC) guarantees the fixed-time synchronization of voltage and frequency for DGs with coordinated power sharing control. Finally, the simulation results validate the control strategy’s effectiveness, robustness to load changes, plug-and-play capability, and indicate that the proposed ET mechanism can greatly decrease communication frequency.

title: Distributed Quantized Control for Multiple DC Microgrids via Asymmetric Sampling Under Bandwidth Constraints
abstract: With the growing digitalization and networking of microgrids, limited bandwidth has become a critical constraint in practical implementation. This paper investigates the problem of distributed control for multiple DC microgrids under bandwidth constraints and proposes a novel control strategy based on dynamic quantization and asymmetric sampling mechanism. The dynamic quantization dynamically adjusts the quantization resolution, enabling efficient communication with as few as 1 bit per transmission, minimizing the required data volume. Meanwhile, the asymmetric sampling allows heterogeneous sampling rates for different generators, substantially decreasing the communication frequency. Unlike event-triggered methods, this strategy avoids the reliance on continuous monitoring devices, thereby enhancing practical feasibility. The proposed control strategy effectively achieves voltage regulation and current sharing among all distributed generators, while enabling power sharing across multiple microgrids under low-bandwidth conditions. Finally, the effectiveness is validated through RT-LAB, demonstrating a 64.43% reduction in bandwidth compared with the baseline event-triggered control strategy, while improving conventional bounded error to zero steady-state error.

title: World-Model-Based Deep Reinforcement Learning for Real-Time Microgrid Energy Management
abstract: This paper proposes a model-based deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework for microgrid energy management built on a Dreamer-style world model. The approach jointly learns a latent dynamics model of the microgrid and a continuous control policy, and uses multi-step imagination rollouts for prediction-based decision making under AC power-flow and operational constraints. Since actions are evaluated inside the learned model before being applied, operators can inspect predicted trajectories to see how decisions affect future costs and network states. The method is tested on three distribution-level microgrids. Across all cases, the proposed method achieves substantially higher sample efficiency than widely adopted model-free RL benchmarks, reaching near-asymptotic performance within a few thousand environment steps while these benchmarks require tens of thousands or fail to converge. The learned policies further achieve a favorable balance between operating cost and safety violations relative to state-of-the-art model-free and model-based RL baselines, approaching the performance of an idealized mixed integer programming-based benchmark with perfect foresight.

title: FedAvgIm: Federated Learning for Multi-Site Impedance Identification of Inverter-Based Resources
abstract: With the increasing integration of inverter-based resources (IBRs) into power systems, assessing small-signal interaction stability has become essential. Impedance/admittance models enable frequency-domain characterization of IBR dynamics without requiring access to proprietary internal control details, but measurement-based identification is time-consuming and must be repeated across operating points. This paper proposes FedAvgIm, a privacy-aware federated-learning framework for multi-site dq-admittance identification under severe local data scarcity and raw-data-locality constraints. Each IBR site trains a local feed-forward neural network using a small set of operating-point–frequency samples, while only model parameters are shared with a cloud aggregator that performs sample-size-weighted FedAvg to update a global model and broadcast it back to all sites. To demonstrate effectiveness, EMT measurement-based admittance datasets are constructed for nine grid-following IBRs with different parameters, architectures, measurement-noise levels, and non-IID settings, where each client has only 40–390 training samples. Results show that FedAvgIm achieves performance close to centralized training and consistently outperforms local-only learning and raw-data-locality-preserving transfer-learning baselines. Additional studies show that FedAvgIm maintains stable learning behavior under measurement noise and remains beneficial under moderate non-IID conditions. The estimated dq-admittance models are further applied to generalized Nyquist stability analysis and validated against EMT time-domain simulations under multiple operating points and grid-strength conditions.

title: Physics-Guided Data-Driven Power Flow Modeling for Unbalanced Distribution Feeders Without Phasor Measurements
abstract: Accurate power-flow (PF) modeling in medium-voltage distribution feeders is challenging due to incomplete physical parameters, for which data-driven approaches provide a flexible and effective solution. However, available data are mostly scalar measurements from transformer low-voltage sides without phase angles. In three-phase three-wire (3P3W) feeders, strong inter-phase coupling caused by line mutual impedances and transformer connections further limits the accuracy of purely data-driven models. Although physics-guided methods have demonstrated strong robustness to measurement errors in vector-domain modeling, effective mechanisms for incorporating physical guidance under scalar measurements are still lacking. To address this gap, this paper proposes a physics-guided data-driven scalar PF model. The model establishes equivalent scalar mappings that characterize feeder and transformer coupling, embedding this physical guidance into the data-driven regression process. Case studies demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves high accuracy, robustness, and physical consistency, ensuring reliable PF estimation even under large measurement errors and strong phase-coupling conditions.

title: A Probabilistic Graph Reinforcement Learning for Resilient Service Restoration via Microgrid Formation
abstract: Service restoration in distribution systems after major outages is a complex and time-sensitive task under significant uncertainty and high penetration of distributed energy resources (DERs). Conventional deep reinforcement learning (DRL) methods typically rely on Markov decision processes (MDPs) and Euclidean state representations, limiting their ability to capture stochastic temporal dynamics and network topology. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a probabilistic graph reinforcement learning framework for microgrid formation. The restoration problem is formulated as a semi-Markov decision process (SMDP) to explicitly model stochastic state sojourn times. A Bayesian graph convolutional network is developed to jointly capture spatial dependencies and parameter uncertainty. Building on this, a novel Bayesian graph soft actor-critic (BGSAC) algorithm is proposed, where the entropy regularization coefficient is adaptively adjusted based on uncertainty estimates, enhancing exploration capability and robustness in uncertain environments. Experimental results on the IEEE 123-bus system demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing DRL approaches in convergence stability and final performance. Moreover, compared with optimization-based and heuristic baselines, it achieves comparable restoration effectiveness with substantially reduced decision time, highlighting its suitability for real-time service restoration.

title: A Causal-Guided Multimodal Large Language Model for Generalized Power System Time-Series Data Analytics
abstract: Power system time series analytics is critical in understanding the system operation conditions and predicting the future trends. Despite the wide adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools, many AI-based time series analytical models suffer from task-specificity (i.e., one model for one task) and structural rigidity (i.e., the input-output format is fixed), leading to limited model performance and resource waste. In this paper, we propose a Causal-Guided Multimodal Large Language Model (CM-LLM) that can solve heterogeneous power system time-series analysis tasks. First, we introduce a physics-statistics combined causal discovery mechanism to capture the causal relationship, which is represented by a graph, among power system variables. Second, we propose a multimodal data preprocessing framework that can encode and fuse text, graph and time series to enhance the model performance. Last, we formulate a generic “mask-and-reconstruct” paradigm and design a dynamic input-output padding mechanism to enable CM-LLM to adapt to heterogeneous time-series analysis tasks with varying sample lengths. Simulation results based on open-source LLM Qwen and real-world datasets demonstrate that, after simple fine-tuning, the proposed CM-LLM can achieve satisfying accuracy and efficiency on three heterogeneous time-series analytics tasks: missing data imputation, forecasting and super resolution.

title: Unsupervised Lightweight Transfer Learning for Edge Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring
abstract: Non-intrusive load monitoring (NILM) is crucial for residential real-time energy management as it provides appliance-level consumption insights. Deploying NILM at the edge enables immediate feedback and preserves user privacy by processing data locally. While deep learning has significantly advanced NILM, its direct deployment on the edge faces major hurdles. The deep learning models are often too large to be applied to resource-constrained hardware. In addition, their performance may degrade substantially for a new household due to cross-household domain shifts. To overcome these two obstacles, this paper presents a novel lightweight transfer learning framework consisting of two main phases: dynamic network compression (DNC) and lightweight cross-domain transfer (LCT). DNC enables the progressive shrinking training of an elastic supernet in the cloud, which can be flexibly compressed into compact subnets tailored to the memory constraints of various edge devices without retraining. LCT enables efficient fine-tuning of deployed subnets at the edge in an unsupervised manner, adapting them to locally unlabeled cross-domain data by only updating lightweight residual modules. Experiments on a hardware testbed demonstrate that the proposed framework significantly outperforms existing methods in both disaggregation accuracy and memory efficiency, demonstrating its capability to deliver high-performance NILM on various edge devices.

title: Carbon-Aware V2G Coordination in PV-Rich Distribution Systems via Weather-Incorporated Two-Stage Graph Reinforcement Learning and Data Distillation
abstract: The increasing penetration of photovoltaic (PV) generation introduces significant volatility and PV-load temporal mismatch into power distribution systems, necessitating advanced strategies to maintain efficient and sustainable operation. While vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology presents a promising solution by leveraging electric vehicle (EV) fleets as distributed energy storage, coordinating a large fleet of EVs for PV-rich distribution systems remains a complex, high-dimensional problem. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a novel weather-incorporated two-stage graph reinforcement learning approach based on data distillation for carbon-aware V2G coordination. In the first stage, stochastic operational data, including PV generation and load profiles, are distilled according to weather and day types to simplify data patterns. The resulting distilled profiles are then used to pre-train a guidance policy. At the second stage, the pre-trained guidance policy facilitates more effective policy learning for the refined policy by providing guidance actions, enabling it to efficiently handle stochasticity in the original operational data and thereby improving overall learning performance. To further enhance the adaptability of V2G coordination, we design a hierarchical graph neural network (HGNN) that learns spatiotemporal correlations involved in the V2G coordination problem and effectively adapts to changes in system configuration, such as the addition or removal of charging stations, without requiring retraining. Evaluations are conducted on a modified PV-rich IEEE 33-bus system incorporating multiple charging stations, demonstrating its suitability for practical deployment in PV-rich distribution systems.

title: Learning-Free Laplacian Kernel Modeling for Joint Imputation of Multi-Energy Load Data in Integrated Energy Systems
abstract: The reliability of data-driven applications in integrated energy systems (IESs), such as multi-energy load prediction, relies on the availability of complete and high-quality load data. However, real-world multi-energy load data can suffer from missing records, and accurate recovery remains challenging due to heterogeneous missing patterns and strong yet nontrivial coupling among different energy loads. To address this issue, this paper proposes an efficient learning-free Laplacian kernel framework for joint multi-energy load imputation, in which missing entries are directly treated as decision variables and the complete load matrix is reconstructed through a unified convex optimization formulation without requiring any training data. The proposed framework captures both the intra-load structure and cross-load coupling of multi-energy load data. This is achieved by combining a circulant Laplacian kernel-based temporal regularizer and a circulant tensor nuclear norm for local continuity and global periodicity, respectively, together with a correlation-based signed Laplacian regularizer for inter-load coupling relationship modeling. To efficiently solve the resulting optimization problem, an alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithm is derived, where the dominant updates are implemented in the frequency domain via the fast Fourier transform (FFT) by exploiting the underlying circulant structures. This enables fast and scalable imputation of long-horizon and high-resolution load data with low computational overhead. Numerical experiments on real-world multi-energy load datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework not only consistently outperforms state-of-the-art imputation baselines under different missing patterns but also yields superior performance in downstream load forecasting tasks. The source code is available at: https://github.com/zhaopengfei12345/data-imputation

title: A Unified Virtual Battery Modeling Framework for Flexibility Characterization of Building HVAC Systems
abstract: The heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems dominate building’s energy consumption and meanwhile exhibit substantial operational flexibility that can be exploited for providing grid services. However, this goal is largely hindered by the difficulty to characterize the system’s operating flexibility due to the complex building thermal dynamics, physical operating limits and human comfort constraints. To address this challenge, this paper develops a unified virtual battery (VB) modeling framework for characterizing the operating flexibility of both single-zone and multi-zone building HVAC systems, enabling responsive buildings to function like virtual batteries. Specifically, a physically meaningful representation state is first identified to represent building thermal conditions under thermal comfort constraints and then a VB model is established for characterizing the operating flexibility of single-zone HVAC systems. We subsequently extend the VB modeling framework to multi-zone HVAC systems and establish zone VB models to characterize the heterogeneous zonal operating flexibility. We further develop a systematic method to aggregate the zone VB models into a unified VB model. The proposed VB model enables a low-order storage-like representation of the operational flexibility of both single-zone and multi-zone buildings. Case studies demonstrate that the VB model can well capture the building thermal dynamics under varying HVAC control policies. In addition, the VB model is validated through demand response (DR) of buildings. The optimal DR strategies can be obtained from the low-order and low-complexity VB model, and the building’s committed DR can be efficiently decomposed to zone-level control inputs while maintaining human thermal comfort.

title: Robust Unknown Input Observer-Based Estimation and Mitigation Against Sensor Spoofing Attacks in Cyber-Physical Microgrids
abstract: Microgrids are increasingly dependent on real-time sensing and network communication for the monitoring and control of distributed energy resources (DERs), exposing them to numerous cyber attacks such as sensor spoofing. In such attacks, additive biases are injected into sensor measurements without directly spoofing the communication network and control logic. Conventional observer-based bias estimation methods face several challenges. They typically rely on accurate system models, and their estimation performance deteriorates in the presence of system uncertainties, including parameter uncertainties, process and measurement noise, and unknown inputs. These factors make sensor spoofing-induced biases difficult to distinguish from normal state variations, causing interaction between sensor biases and system uncertainties and leading to degraded control performance in practical microgrid operation. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a Robust Unknown Input Observer (RUIO) for the accurate estimation of sensor spoofing-induced biases in the presence of various system uncertainties. The sensor bias is modeled as an augmented state, and the observer gain is synthesized using Linear Matrix Inequality (LMI) optimization under an ${\mathcal {H}}_{\infty } $ performance criterion to ensure robustness against system uncertainties. Given the structural observability limitation of the Unknown Input Observer (UIO) formulation, which prevents simultaneous estimation of independent current and voltage sensor biases, an event-triggered bias estimation and mitigation framework is designed to counter any single sensor spoofing attack. The dual-RUIO scheme is switched adaptively based on the current-sharing error after mitigation, with an appropriate holding interval incorporated to ensure stable operation. The effectiveness of the proposed RUIO-based framework is validated through extensive experiments on a cyber-physical microgrid testbed. Comparative evaluations against conventional state estimation methods demonstrate improved estimation accuracy and mitigation performance.

title: Nonlinear PDE-Constrained Optimal Dispatch of Gas and Power: A Global Linearization Approximation
abstract: The coordinated dispatch of power and gas is fundamental for the operational security of Electricity-Gas Integrated Energy Systems (EG-IES). However, the gas dynamics in the natural gas system (NGS) are governed by the nonlinear partial differential equations (PDE), making the dispatch problem of the EG-IES a complicated optimization model constrained by nonlinear PDE. Inaccurate modeling, such as the commonly used locally linearized model, can lead to operational limit violations in the NGS that might propagate and threaten the security of the coupled power system. To address it, we propose a globally linearized gas network model based on the Koopman operator theory. In particular, we propose a data-driven Koopman operator approximation approach for the globally linearized gas network model based on the extended dynamic mode decomposition, in which a physics-informed stability constraint is derived and embedded to improve generalization and accuracy. Based on this foundation, we develop an optimal dispatch model for the EG-IES. For the first time, this model explicitly incorporates the nonlinear gas dynamics governed by PDEs without resorting to local linearization or spatial discretization. The case study verifies the effectiveness of this work. Simulation results reveal that the commonly used locally linearized gas network model fails to accurately capture the dynamic characteristics of NGS, bringing potential security threats to the system.

title: Privacy-Preserving Decision-Focused Learning for Multi-Energy Systems
abstract: Decision-making for multi-energy system (MES) dispatch depends on accurate load forecasting. Traditionally, load forecasting and decision-making for MES are implemented separately. Forecasting models are typically trained to minimize forecasting errors, overlooking their impact on downstream decision-making. To address this, decision-focused learning (DFL) has been studied to minimize decision-making costs instead. However, practical adoption of DFL in MES faces significant challenge: the process requires sharing sensitive load data and model parameters across multiple sectors, raising serious privacy issues. To this end, we propose a privacy-preserving DFL framework tailored for MES. Our approach introduces information masking to safeguard private data while enabling recovery of decision variables and gradients required for model training. To further enhance security for DFL, we design a safety protocol combining matrix decomposition and homomorphic encryption, effectively preventing collusion and unauthorized data access. Additionally, we develop a privacy-preserving load pattern recognition algorithm, that enables the training of specialized DFL models for heterogeneous load patterns. Theoretical analysis and case studies with real-world MES data, demonstrate that our framework not only protects privacy but also consistently achieves lower average daily dispatch costs compared to existing methods.

title: Physics-Embedded Graph Convolutional Network With Topology-Adaptive Transfer Learning for Power Flow Prediction
abstract: Power flow prediction is a growing task in uncertain power system operation and analysis. Although data-driven models which apply machine learning techniques offer computational efficiency for power flow calculation, they often result in physically inconsistent solutions and exhibit poor generalization across different network topologies. This article proposes a physics-embedded graph convolutional network (PE-GCN) for physically consistent power flow prediction, and further develops a topology-adaptive transfer learning framework to improve generalization across different power network topologies. PE-GCN is developed based on a reformulated bus injection model (BIM) and embeds physical laws into the network architecture and training process. Specifically, hard constraints are enforced through a nodal power balance correction layer, and soft constraints are incorporated during training via a physics-regularized loss to enhance physical consistency. Building on PE-GCN, a topology-adaptive transfer learning framework with adversarial domain adaptation is introduced to improve generalization across network topologies and reduce the reliance on extensive labeled data under topology variations. Numerical studies on the IEEE-30, IEEE-118, and IEEE-300 bus systems validate the effectiveness of the proposed method in terms of prediction accuracy, physical consistency, computational efficiency, and adaptability to topology variations.

title: Hierarchical Operation of Large-Scale Multi-Energy Systems With Real-Time V2G and Heat Pump Control
abstract: In this paper, we present a real-time control strategy for large-scale Multi-Energy Systems (MES) with coupled electrical, thermal, and gas networks. A novel hierarchical operator-to-operator framework is proposed to coordinate flexible resources, such as Electric Vehicles (EVs) in Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) mode and Heat Pumps (HPs), to mitigate operational challenges in MES. Accounting for V2G peculiarities, including four-quadrant operation, EV driver behaviour, and V2G agreements, we show how EVs can function as flexible storage units that provide ancillary services such as voltage regulation, loss reduction, and cost minimization. Moreover, HPs equipped with thermal storage cooperate with V2G to enhance flexibility and improve energy efficiency across coupled sectors. A realistic large-scale MES based on our research center infrastructure (Forschungszentrum Jülich) is used for validation. Results indicate that the hierarchical framework enables scalable real-time coordination of numerous EVs and HPs under practical constraints, confirming its suitability for large-scale MES.

title: Real-Time Measurement of Transition Resistance and Full-Time Fault Feeder Selection for Random Arc-Fault in Active Distribution Networks
abstract: Single-phase-to-ground fault occurs frequently in active distribution network, often accompanied by nonlinear arc, and the fault development trend changes instantaneously and randomly. However, the existing fault detection methods for stable faults or specific arc faults are difficult to work in practical fault conditions. To achieve real-time tracking of the fault development trend, precise identification of fault types, and reliable selection of fault feeder for random faults occurring in complex and diverse environments, a novel method for real-time measurement of transition resistance and full-time fault feeder selection is proposed in this paper. Firstly, an equivalent circuit diagram of the active distribution network is established considering the parameter asymmetry and damping ratio, to acquire the current flowing through the transition resistance and the voltage across it in real time. Subsequently, the transition resistances of various types of faults are measured in real time based on Ohm’s law, and the stability, periodicity and mutation characteristics of the measured transition resistance are utilized to accurately identify the fault type and track its development trend. Finally, the zero-sequence current is decomposed to eliminate, as much as possible, components irrelevant to fault feeder selection. This process ensures that the characteristic waveforms of the fault feeder and normal feeders remain in opposite phases throughout the entire time period, thereby preventing selection failures caused by the loss of critical transient information. Simulation and 10kV experimental platform prove the feasibility of the proposed methods.

title: Vision of Future Smart Control Center: Fusion of Large Language Models and Power System Intelligent Computing
abstract: The high stochasticity of renewable dominated power grids demands advanced dispatch strategies. However, the disparity between flexible operator intent and rigid legacy tools hinders resilient system operation. To address this challenge,this paper proposes a future smart control center architecture that fuses Large Language Models (LLMs) with Power System Intelligent Computing (PSIC). In this architecture, the LLM functions as the cognitive core for intent understanding, workflow orchestration, and causal reasoning. Concurrently, PSIC executes physical simulations and data-driven optimization tasks decomposed by the LLM. This integration creates a cognitive decision-making process where the adaptive decision-making capability enabled by LLM is rigorously bounded and verified by physical laws. Consequently, the architecture enables next generation human-machine collaborative dispatch, advancing grid operations from automation toward true intelligence and self-evolution.

title: Learning-Augmented Mixed-Integer Reformulation for Dynamic Traffic and Energy Assignment in Spatio-Temporal V2G Coordination
abstract: The increasing integration of electric vehicles (EVs) enables grid services through spatio-temporal vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology. While prior studies have explored dynamic traffic assignment (DTA) for EV charging management, most existing DTA formulations treat charging and discharging power as exogenous or fixed parameters, limiting V2G flexibility utilization and coordination. This work proposes a learning-augmented mixed-integer reformulation for dynamic traffic and energy assignment (DTEA) that co-optimizes EV traffic flows and continuous (dis)charging power. Specifically, to address the nonlinear flow-power coupling terms, we develop a structure-preserving constraint learning-based method that replicates only the nonlinear coupling terms while retaining the operational constraints. The trained neural networks (NNs) are embedded into the optimization model through tractable mixed-integer reformulations, and data-driven local trust-region restrictions are introduced to mitigate extrapolation risk and improve solution reliability. Case studies demonstrate the effectiveness, scalability, and robustness of the proposed solution method.

title: Generative Autonomous Grid Control: Integrating Decision Transformers With a Two-Stage Safety Stack
abstract: The displacement of synchronous generation by inverter-based resources is accelerating power system frequency dynamics beyond the response capability of conventional automatic generation control. This paper presents Autonomous Grid Generation Control with Decision Transformers, a framework coupling an offline-trained Decision Transformer with a two-stage symbolic safety stack for secondary frequency control. The Decision Transformer learns a conditional dispatch policy from offline supervisory control and data acquisition records via sequence modeling, eliminating online exploration risks. A Constraint Verification Unit provides sub-ten-millisecond algebraic screening using real-time power transfer distribution factors, while an aggregate digital twin performs swing-equation-based dynamic stability certification. Validated on the Northeast Power Coordinating Council 140-bus system under low-inertia conditions, the proposed controller reduces the area control error integral by over 99% relative to tuned automatic generation control, maintains a 59.4 Hz frequency nadir, and achieves inference latency of approximately 10 ms, well within real-time constraints. Comparative evaluation against a linear quadratic regulator baseline and structural analysis against conservative Q-learning demonstrate the advantages of the sequence-modeling formulation. Small-signal eigenvalue analysis characterizes the dominant 1.87 Hz electromechanical mode and confirms that the safety stack maintains stable operation across operating points. By falling back to tuned automatic generation control whenever proposals are rejected, the safety stack bounds worst-case performance to industry-standard levels in simulation.

title: Online Feasible Region Characterization of Aggregated DERs via Incremental Projection
abstract: Performing fast and accurate feasible region characterization (FRC) for aggregated distributed energy resources (DERs) is essential for real-time operational dispatching. Affected by the temporal coupling and the uncertainty associated with DERs, the aggregated feasible regions exhibit high-dimensional coupling and strong stochasticity. However, existing methods cannot quickly perform accurate FRC of the entire operational domain, resulting in preventing real-time updating of FRC based on rolling forecasts of uncertain sources and loads. To this end, an incremental projection-based online full-time-domain FRC method is proposed in this paper, which requires only a local projection of the forecasts to achieve fast and accurate FRC. First, the reversible decoupling equivalent reformulation is developed to decompose the original high-dimensional FRC into several sliced low-dimensional FRCs, while the temporal coupling feature is retained. Then, to shorten the computation time, a universal incremental projection paradigm is constructed, in which the whole FRC is quickly updated by replacing local projections in the complete FRC results obtained offline. Statistical analysis validates that the proposed method can reduce the computation time in the order of 0.55% compared to that of the existing techniques without losing accuracy.

title: Secure Prespecified-Time Distributed Energy Management via Dual-Layer Privacy-Preserving Mechanism
abstract: This paper investigates the energy management (EM) problem for microgrids in a fast and secure manner. To rapidly obtain the optimal power output combination, a flexible distributed EM algorithm over digraphs is proposed based on a novel prespecified-time convergence lemma, which enables the presetting of convergence time independent of initial states or algorithmic parameters. Considering the privacy protection of incremental costs (ICs), a new dual-layer privacy-preserving mechanism is devised to defend against both internal honest-but-curious (HBC) distributed generators and external eavesdroppers. The first privacy-preserving layer is state decomposition, which operates throughout the entire scheduling horizon. The second privacy-preserving layer is edge-based additive perturbations, which operates during the coordinated scrambling phase. The state decomposition mechanism divides the ICs into two auxiliary variables, and the additive perturbation method can further protect the privacy of these auxiliary variables. Simulation results are provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed EM strategy.

title: Robust Energy Management for Distributed Energy Resources Using Homothetic Tube-Based Economic Model Predictive Control
abstract: Conventional tube-based model predictive control often suffers from excessive conservatism and sub-optimal economic performance when applied to microgrid energy management due to its reliance on rigid uncertainty bounds. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a novel hierarchical homothetic tube-based economic model predictive control (HT-EMPC) framework for the optimal coordination of distributed energy resources (DERs) under uncertainties. By constructing a nested structure of dynamically scaled tubes for both intraday scheduling and real-time control, the proposed approach accurately characterizes uncertainty propagation and significantly reduces operational conservatism by enlarging the feasible region for nominal optimization. The economic efficiency of the coordination is further enhanced through a vertex-based robust objective function, which tractably evaluates operational costs at the extreme points of the homothetic error tubes to ensure robustness against worst-case state deviations. Furthermore, the framework is supported by a rigorous theoretical analysis that provides a formal guarantee of robust state invariance, confirming the system’s recursive feasibility and safety against fast-varying real-time disturbances. Comparative studies on microgrid systems validate that the proposed HT-EMPC strategy achieves a superior balance between adaptive robustness and economic performance compared to both nominal and rigid-tube MPC benchmarks.

title: A Robust Control Framework for Smooth Operation of PV-Integrated Weak Grids
abstract: The integration of photovoltaic (PV) systems into weak grids poses significant challenges to ensure smooth and stable operation. This paper proposes a robust control framework to ensure the smooth operation of PV-integrated weak grids. The system employs a grid-tied PV generation system sharing a common DC link with a distribution static compensator (DSTATCOM). A hybrid backstepping and barrier function-based sliding mode controller is developed as the core of this framework, serving a dual purpose: it manages the PV generation system for maximum power point tracking and DC-link voltage regulation, while simultaneously controlling the DSTATCOM to mitigate power quality issues. The controller’s robustness is demonstrated through its ability to minimize errors in critical parameters (<inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$V_{pv}$ </tex-math></inline-formula>, <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$V_{dc}$ </tex-math></inline-formula>, <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$I_{d}$ </tex-math></inline-formula>, and <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$I_{q}$ </tex-math></inline-formula>). The framework’s performance is exhaustively evaluated under both linear and nonlinear load conditions via MATLAB/Simulink simulations and validated on a laboratory-scale hardware prototype. A comparative analysis with standard PID and SMC techniques confirms the superiority of the proposed framework, showing significant improvements in total harmonic distortion reduction to 2.18% under linear and 2.46% under nonlinear load conditions, alongside enhanced voltage regulation. The results affirm that the proposed robust control framework is highly effective for maintaining stable, high-quality power in PV-integrated weak grids.

title: Joint Robust and Chance-Constrained Optimization for Pre-Disaster Hardening Strategy of Power-Thermal Cyber-Physical Systems
abstract: The integration of large-scale distributed photovoltaics (PVs) introduces significant operational uncertainties in urban power-thermal cyber-physical systems (PTCPS), particularly during typhoon events, which pose severe risks to system safety. Distribution-based models, such as chance constraints, effectively handle PV uncertainties. However, under extreme typhoon events, the scarcity of component fault data limits the availability of distribution knowledge, thereby reducing their effectiveness. To overcome this challenge, a joint robust and chance-constrained optimization (JRCCO) framework for pre-disaster coordinated hardening of PTCPS is proposed. The framework incorporates parameter distribution knowledge and uncertainty sets to minimize safety investment costs. Notably, multi-region sequential fault decision-dependent uncertainty (DDU) sets, designed to operate without requiring distribution knowledge, are introduced alongside chance constraints for PV output. To address the nonlinearity in chance constraints, a linearization method combining chance capacity and Cornish-Fisher series expansion is developed. Moreover, to improve computational efficiency and universality, a modified relaxed column-and-constraint generation with robust cuts (MRCCG-RC) algorithm is developed, which is complemented by acceleration techniques and supported by theoretical proofs. Two PTCPS of different scales are tested, showing that the strategy can reduce hardening costs by 19.15% and load shedding by 41.61%, effectively enhancing the PTCPS’s performance against typhoon disasters.

title: Equilibrium Scheduling Strategy for MSOP via Bayesian Dynamic Segmentation of Complementarity Among LVDNs
abstract: Mobile Soft Open Point (MSOP) technology improves the flexibility and utilization of interconnection resources by enabling mobile deployment across low-voltage distribution networks (LVDNs). However, efficient MSOP scheduling depends on accurately identifying the stage-wise complementarity among interconnectable LVDNs under time-varying source-load conditions. This paper proposes a bi-level equilibrium scheduling framework for MSOP by integrating stage-wise complementarity segmentation with coordinated scheduling optimization. First, a Gaussian mixture model is used to construct the complementary probability matrix among LVDNs, and Bayesian dynamic segmentation is employed to identify statistically stable complementarity stages from its temporal evolution. Then, by incorporating the segmented complementarity stages as stage-wise inputs, a bi-level MSOP scheduling model is developed to coordinate the trade-off between the net benefit of MSOP and the mobile scheduling cost. The scheduling problem is formulated as a Pareto-Nash-equilibrium-based multi-objective coordinated optimization problem. Simulation results verify the effectiveness of the proposed method.

title: Hybrid Attention-Augmented Self-Interpretable Channel-Grouped Graph Convolutional Network for Robust Distribution Network Fault Diagnosis
abstract: Deep learning (DL)-based methods have illustrated excellent performance in distribution network fault diagnosis. However, the “opaque” nature of DL models hinders grid operators from understanding the decision-making processes of these models, affecting model trustworthiness and robustness in diversified diagnosis applications. This paper proposes a hybrid attention-augmented self-interpretable channel-grouped graph convolutional network (HASIG) for diverse short-circuit fault diagnosis of distribution networks, including binary fault detection, faulted line identification, and fault type classification. A channel-grouped graph convolutional network is proposed to learn features from three-phase voltage and current measurements. We present a hybrid attention that combines global edge attention and channel-grouped attention, which can augment the critical features with faithful and robust interpretations during model training, enabling users to gain insights into the predictive behavior inside the model. These three short-circuit fault diagnosis tasks are collaboratively trained under a multi-task learning architecture with interpretable loss constraints. Experiments were conducted on the IEEE 33-bus, IEEE 33-bus with distributed energy resources, and IEEE 123-bus systems with randomized fault parameters. The results show that HASIG achieves competitive diagnostic performance and good interpretability, and demonstrates strong robustness under noisy and missing-data conditions.

title: Incentive-Compatible Online Pricing of Customer Directrix Load-Based Demand Response for Load Aggregators
abstract: In demand response (DR) programs, load aggregators (LAs) coordinate DR customers to provide flexibility support for the smart grid. However, existing pricing mechanisms often struggle to simultaneously achieve incentive compatibility and operational controllability in retail-side DR. To address this challenge, this paper proposes an incentive compatible online pricing strategy for customer directrix load (CDL)-based DR of LAs. Unlike traditional price-based DR schemes, the proposed approach leverages CDL, which inherently enhances controllability by serving as both the guiding signal and the performance evaluation metric. Within the CDL framework, a DR customer response model and an LA centralized optimization model are established. Under a general discomfort function setting, the centralized response is characterized by a one-dimensional fixed-point equation, based on which a customized incentive compatible pricing strategy is derived to align individual customer responses with the LA’s desired response curve. Furthermore, the widely used quadratic discomfort model is studied as an analytically tractable special case, leading to closed-form response and pricing expressions. An online learning algorithm is then proposed to enable LAs to learn the unobservable discomfort parameters of DR customers from observable response decisions, thereby reducing information exposure and enhancing practical implementation performance. The proposed algorithm is theoretically shown to achieve logarithmic regret with respect to the operating cycle, and a problem-level regret lower bound is further established to show that the minimax cumulative regret of the underlying CDL-based online pricing problem is also logarithmic. Simulation results based on real-world data demonstrate the validity and effectiveness of the proposed method.

title: Unstable Oscillatory Modes Estimation in the Frequency Domain
abstract: Although frequency-domain analysis is a powerful tool for small-signal stability assessment in power systems, its sensitivity analyses generally aim at selected frequencies, particularly around poorly damped or undamped modes. However, reliably identifying the unstable frequencies within the frequency-domain framework remains a significant challenge. This work introduces and demonstrates a robust method based on the Generalized Nyquist Criterion for estimating unstable oscillatory frequencies, which overcomes the exposed limitations of existing techniques.

title: Contrastive Preference Learning From User Overrides for Personalized Home Energy Management
abstract: Personalizing home energy management systems (HEMSs) to align with dynamic user preferences remains challenging for intelligent energy control. Existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approaches typically rely on static reward functions and fixed constraints, limiting their ability to adapt to diverse user behaviors. We propose a framework that leverages user override feedback—instances where users manually correct system decisions—as implicit preference signals. Our method combines contrastive preference learning from pairwise comparisons, context-aware preference embeddings from interaction history, and preference-conditioned DRL policies. This enables the controller to continuously align with personalized preferences without explicit reward engineering. Validation on real-world residential energy data shows that the framework achieves an average override rate of 0.033 across four diverse preference profiles—a 37% reduction over the strongest baseline—while maintaining the lowest user interaction cost (0.394) among all feedback-driven methods. The framework also demonstrates efficient transfer across prototype preferences and generalization to novel behavioral rules.

title: A Data-Driven Probabilistic Harmonic Current Forecasting for Aggregated Harmonic Sources
abstract: With the increasing deployment of non-linear power electronic devices in distribution networks, the issue of excessive harmonics has become increasingly prominent. Accurate analysis and forecasting of harmonic currents are essential to better understand and mitigate harmonic-related problems. Common harmonic sources in power grids include various types of loads and renewable energy generation equipment, such as wind and photovoltaic systems. Accordingly, this paper focuses on forecasting harmonic currents for different types of aggregated harmonic sources. Considering the strong randomness, high time-variability, and coupling characteristics of harmonic currents, a data-driven probabilistic harmonic current forecasting method is proposed. First, the raw data are decomposed into deterministic and stochastic components. Next, a radial basis function autoregressive exponential model is employed to perform point forecasting of the deterministic component, accommodating multiple input factors and simultaneous multi-harmonic outputs while preserving model partial interpretability. Subsequently, the proposed multi-Gaussian fitting method and an improved Markov chain Monte Carlo approach are used for probabilistic forecasting of the stochastic component. Finally, the deterministic and stochastic component predictions are combined to yield the final probabilistic harmonic current forecast. Using actual harmonic measurement data, comparative analyses with multiple intelligent models are conducted to validate the effectiveness and accuracy of the proposed forecasting method. Furthermore, the harmonic current predictions are applied to forward probabilistic harmonic power flows, and corresponding forward and new probabilistic harmonic mitigation measures are proposed, demonstrating practical engineering applicability.

title: Multi-Timescale Transmission-Distribution Coordination Under Decision-Dependent Uncertainty for Enhancing Economic Performance and Operational Reliability
abstract: Coordinated operation between the transmission network (TN) and distribution networks (DNs) is essential to accommodate the high penetration of distributed photovoltaic (PV). Two gaps remain in TN-DN coordination regarding multi-timescale scheduling and decision-dependent uncertainty (DDU) management. This paper proposes a multi-timescale TN-DN coordinated operation framework, which together provides DDU-aware uncertainty modeling and algorithm design. First, the framework architecture is presented, which includes a day-ahead stage at an hourly resolution and an intra-day stage at a 15-minute resolution. Then, the optimal day-ahead TN-DN coordinated scheduling strategy is developed, which includes day-ahead operation and hourly TN-DN power exchanges. Herein, an improved consensus alternating direction method of multipliers (C-ADMM) is proposed to accelerate the convergence of the multi-timescale TN-DN coordinated operation framework. Finally, the intra-day TN-DN scheduling model is formulated, in which a chance-constrained optimization is adopted to capture DDU characteristics for DNs. The chance constraints are further reformulated as robust constraints via a robust approximation approach to guarantee solution tractability. Case studies verify that the proposed framework increases the accommodation of distributed PV while enhancing the economic performance and operational reliability of ITDS.

title: A Novel Synchrophasor Post-Processing Method for Uploading in Distribution Networks Based on Sparse Decomposition
abstract: The large-scale integration of distributed power generations and other power electronic devices into the power grid introduces new challenges for the control and dispatching of distribution networks. Synchrophasor measurements can provide real-time data to meet control requirements. However, the widespread adoption of synchrophasor measurement technology in distribution networks is limited due to several factors such as communication constraints and deployment costs. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an optimized sparse decomposition method for synchrophasor uploading, aimed at characterizing slow dynamic processes with a lower reporting rate. First, an improved Gabor overcomplete dictionary is designed to better capture both the periodicity and abrupt changes in signals within distribution networks. Then, to more efficiently match the optimal atom, the matching pursuit process is enhanced using a Modified Sine-Cosine Algorithm (MSCA). This enhancement is achieved through the optimized initialization of candidate solutions and the application of nonlinear adjustments to control parameters, resulting in improved decomposition efficiency and reconstruction accuracy. Furthermore, the proposed method is implemented on Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGA) to enhance the execution parallelism of the algorithm, laying the groundwork for future development of low-cost custom chips suitable for widespread deployment in distribution networks. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that the proposed method can process 100 frames of synchrophasor data within 0.1 seconds, reducing the data volume by over 87% compared to uncompressed transmission. Moreover, it consistently delivers a compression ratio at least 1.5 times higher than benchmark methods across varying data volumes.

title: A Graph Neural Network With Auxiliary Task Learning for Missing PMU Data Reconstruction
abstract: In wide-area measurement systems (WAMS), phasor measurement unit (PMU) measurement is prone to data missing due to hardware failures, communication delays, and cyber-attacks. Existing data-driven methods are limited by poor adaptability to concept drift in power systems, poor robustness under high missing rates, and reliance on the unrealistic assumption of full system observability. Thus, this paper proposes an auxiliary task learning (ATL) method for reconstructing missing PMU data. First, a K-hop graph neural network (GNN) is proposed to enable direct learning on the subgraph consisting of PMU nodes, overcoming the limitation of the incompletely observable system. Then, an auxiliary learning framework consisting of two complementary graph networks is designed for accurate reconstruction: a spatial-temporal GNN extracts spatial-temporal dependencies from PMU data to reconstruct missing values, and another auxiliary GNN utilizes the low-rank property of PMU data to achieve unsupervised online learning. In this way, the low-rank properties of the PMU data are dynamically leveraged across the architecture to ensure robustness and self-adaptation. Numerical results demonstrate the superior offline and online performance of the proposed method under high missing rates and incomplete observability.

title: Analytical Framework for Assessing Effective Regional Inertia
abstract: This paper proposes a novel formulation of effective regional inertia that explicitly accounts for both system topology and the spatial distribution of inertia. Unlike traditional approaches that model a region as an aggregated machine with an equivalent inertia, the proposed metric provides a topology-aware representation. The methodology builds on an analytical framework that extends classical slow coherency theory to address network partitioning and regional frequency stability. Based on these partitions, we develop a systematic procedure to evaluate the effective inertia of each region, enabling a more accurate interpretation of local inertial contributions, including those from virtual inertia provided by inverter-based resources (IBRs). Case studies on the IEEE 39-bus, 68-bus, and a reduced version of the Brazilian Interconnected system demonstrate that the integration of inertial devices does not uniformly improve system frequency response, underscoring the importance of the proposed metric for effective regional inertia assessment.

title: Frequency-Spectra Impedance Margin Ratio for Stability Analysis of IBR-Penetrated Systems
abstract: The soaring penetration of inverter-based resources (IBRs) in modern power systems creates an urgent need for efficient, model-free methods that provide a systematic stability analysis. Existing approaches fall short in terms of mechanistic insight and feasibility for local measurement. This paper develops a comprehensive frequency-spectra-driven framework for large-scale IBR-penetrated power systems. It establishes sensitivity relationships among the impedance, the determinant and the oscillatory mode along the imaginary frequency axis, providing an efficient guideline for stability improvement. Then, the frequency-spectra impedance margin ratio (fIMR) is proposed to assess the stability margins at each point of interconnection (POI). Stability analysis of massive IBRs is performed solely based on impedance frequency spectra, without requiring the mode identification. Furthermore, compared with the Nyquist stability criterion, the fIMR provides a unified metric for evaluating the stability margins of all POIs, using only the local diagonal impedance blocks. The proposed fIMR method is verified in the modified IEEE systems, where it successfully identifies the weak points and guides the impedance reshaping.

title: A Pseudo-Transient-Enhanced Trajectory-Unified Method for Deterministically Computing Multiple ACOPF Solutions: Methods and Computation
abstract: The feasible region of Alternating Current Optimal Power Flow (ACOPF) models often comprises multiple disjoint feasible components. Each feasible component may contain one or more local optimal solutions (LOSs). Conventional ACOPF solution methodologies typically compute only a single OPF solution and may thereby overlook potential high-value alternative OPF solutions. This paper presents a deterministic numerical method, PGS-TT, to systematically compute all LOSs within each feasible component. PGS-TT integrates the Projected Gradient System with the Trust-Tech framework. This deterministic four-stage method consists of: 1) converging to an LOS; 2) escaping from the current LOS and moving toward another possible OPF solution; 3) detecting the existence of another LOS; and 4) computing the newly detected OPF solution. The proposed numerical PGS-TT method is enhanced by several novel numerical schemes designed to ensure computational efficiency and scalability for large-scale ACOPF models. The method’s effectiveness is demonstrated on several modified IEEE test systems: 118-bus, 500-bus, 1,888-bus, and 30,000-bus. Notably, numerical studies reveal several OPF cases where the higher-cost OPF solution exceeds the lower-cost one by up to 51.45%, highlighting the critical need to compute multiple high-quality LOSs to improve the security and economic efficiency of power system operation and planning.

title: Relative-Degree Wall Restricts Passivity-Based Stability Analysis in Inverter-Dominant Grids
abstract: This letter reveals a fundamental limitation of passivity-based distributed stability analysis in power systems. Under the standard formulation, passivity certification inherently imposes a relative-degree compatibility constraint that excludes many high-fidelity inverter dynamic models (e.g., those that include electromagnetic transients). Potential extensions of passivity frameworks are discussed to break this limitation.

title: Chance-Constrained DC Optimal Power Flow Using Constraint-Informed Statistical Estimation
abstract: Chance-constrained optimization has emerged as a promising framework for managing uncertainties in power systems. This work advances its application to the DC Optimal Power Flow (DC-OPF) model, developing a novel approach to uncertainty modeling and estimation. Current methods typically tackle these problems by first modeling random nodal injections using high-dimensional statistical distributions that scale with the number of buses, followed by deriving deterministic reformulations of the probabilistic constraints. We propose an alternative methodology that exploits the constraint structure to inform the uncertainties to be estimated, enabling significant dimensionality reduction. Rather than learning joint distributions of net-load forecast errors across units, we instead directly model the one-dimensional aggregate system forecast error and two-dimensional line errors weighted by power transfer distribution factors. We evaluate our approach under both Gaussian and non-Gaussian distributions on synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating significant improvements in statistical accuracy and optimization performance compared to existing methods.

title: A Robust Synchronization Method for Enhancing Stability of IBR-Dominated Grids
abstract: Inverter-based resources (IBRs) operating in grid-following (GFL) mode are particularly vulnerable to instabilities in weak grid conditions. This is largely due to the inherent limitations of synchronization with a phase locked loop (PLL). This paper presents a novel voltage magnitude-based synchronization (VMSync) method that ensures stable and well-damped response even in very weak grid conditions, without compromising dynamic performance or adding any stabilization control components. Through comprehensive frequency- and time-domain analysis, VMSync is shown to outperform conventional synchronous reference frame PLL (SRF-PLL) for both small- and large-signal disturbances. Systems with multiple GFL inverters employing VMSync demonstrate significantly improved damping and stability. Furthermore, mixed deployment of VMSync alongside legacy SRF-PLL-based GFL inverters exhibits superior dynamic performance compared to deployment of solely SRF-PLL-based GFL inverters. The results highlight the potential of VMSync as a robust synchronization strategy to mitigate PLL-driven instabilities in power grids with high IBR penetration.

title: Hierarchical Aggregation of Wind Farm Frequency Support Capability Based on Hybrid Control Strategy
abstract: To address the challenge of scalable coordination among massive wind turbines (WTs) managed by different wind farms (WFs) in primary frequency control (PFC), this paper proposes a hierarchical framework for the aggregation and utilization of WF frequency support capability (FSC) to achieve a prescribed frequency performance indicator (PFPI). First, a hybrid control strategy is developed as the control foundation, whose parameters can be reverse-engineered from the PFPI. It enables secondary frequency drop (SFD) mitigation and smooth transition between rotor kinetic energy (RKE)–based support and persistent reserve release. Second, WT-FSC is defined as a WT’s maximum duty factor of the system-level PFC loop within the hybrid control strategy. WT-FSC assessment is formulated as an optimization problem, which considers wake effect, rotor dynamics, WT safety constraints and time-varying system frequency response (SFR) model. Third, to support system-level frequency support service dispatch, WT-level FSC and control cost function are obtained and then aggregated into those of WF-level. Thus, the system operator only needs to make decisions on the duty factors of each WF to optimally utilize all the WT resources. Case studies demonstrate that our framework shows satisfactory assessment accuracy and utilization efficiency of WF-FSC and can enhance system frequency dynamics.

title: Multi-Stage Stochastic Reserve Dispatch via an Adaptive Predispatch-Hazard-Redispatch Framework
abstract: This letter proposes an adaptive predispatch-hazard-redispatch (PHR) framework for multi-stage reserve dispatch in power systems. Unlike existing two-stage predispatch-redispatch and multi-stage heuristic threshold-based approaches, the PHR framework adopts adaptive redispatch weights to balance reserve adequacy assurance and computational cost. The complex multi-stage PHR structure is formulated as a policy graph and solved via a graph stochastic dual dynamic programming approach. Multiple strategies are explored to dynamically adjust redispatch weights based on system flexibility and uncertainty. Case studies on an IEEE 39-bus system demonstrate 70.0–86.5% cost reduction compared to benchmark methods while maintaining computational tractability.

title: Fast and Scalable Newton-Raphson Power Flow Analysis via Hierarchical Parallelism and Graph Node-Based Hash Storage
